newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: German firms hope to regain lost Argentine ground.
newsitem.headline: German firms hope to regain lost Argentine ground.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's visit to Argentina may help German firms recover ground lost on the local league table of foreign investors in the early 1990s, the German-Argentine Chamber of Commerce said Friday.

Otherwise occupied with the reunification of the two Germanies, German companies missed out on the wave of privatizations which saw firms from France, Spain, Britain and the United States stake big claims in Argentina.
"We lost a lot of ground in the privatizations. Now German firms here are finding a much more competitive situation," Chamber president Gerardo Schweiger told a news conference.

The new investors, including France Telecom and Telefonica de Espana, also tend to buy supplies from their home market to fit out their new investments, bypassing German manufacturers, Schweiger said.

Last year, direct German investment in Argentina totaled $200 million. Kohl, who arrives Sunday, will inaugurate a $100 million plant near Buenos Aires built by Mercedes-Benz to assemble its Sprinter van.
While big German companies have long had a presence in Argentina, the next wave of investment is coming from medium-sized and smaller firms, which usually seek out local partners, Schweiger said.
South East Asia has also provided great competition to Latin America in attracting German investment.
Kohl will discuss issues including Argentina's new patents law, which has irritated foreign drugs companies, and the trustworthiness of local courts in enforcing laws and contracts, Schweiger said.
"Judicial security is an issue which worries all industry here, not just German industry," he said.

Another big issue will probably be Argentina's calls for further reductions in European farm subsidies, and access to European markets for Argentine beef. Germany is Argentina's largest beef export market.

Reductions in agricultural subsidies are a major part of talks between the European Union and the Mercosur customs union which aim at an eventual free trade agreement. Mercosur presently groups Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, and the Europeans are keen to gain access to what the Americans have long regarded as their territory.

Representatives from 17 major companies including Mercedes Benz, carmaker Volkswagen, electronics giant Siemens, and chemicals firm Degussa, will accompany Kohl, who will leave for Brazil and Mexico Tuesday.
No new contracts or major agreements are likely to be signed when Kohl is here, apart from a double-taxation treaty.
